method.scale: 1-5, whole numbers only. 5 = the force is strong and squeezes industry profits hard; 1 = the force is weak (written-assignment convention).
method.polarity_conflict: The course reference spreadsheet (self-storage example) scores each force for attractiveness to incumbents: 5 = most attractive (weak force), 1 = least attractive (strong force). The written assignment says the opposite: 5 = the force is strong and squeezes profits, 1 = weak. This tool follows the written assignment. A 4 here is a strong, profit-squeezing force; on the spreadsheet's scale the same force would be about a 2.
method.granularity_conflict: The spreadsheet averages dozens of weighted sub-components into decimal force scores (its example's rivalry is 2.4167) and then averages the five forces with equal 0.2 weights into one overall score (3.39). The assignment requires whole numbers and naming the dominant forces instead of averaging. This tool uses the spreadsheet's sub-dimension categories only as a checklist to make sure each force's facts cover different points. It outputs one whole-number score per force and no sub-scores, and it never averages across forces. Where the judgment was torn between two numbers, the rationale says so.
method.spreadsheet_used_for: Only the standard of evidence depth: each force backed by several specific, cited facts.
method.evidence_rules: Each fact has at least one citation with a verbatim quote of 25 words or fewer. A fact counts only if every quote verifies in code against cached source text; unverified facts are dropped. Each force needs at least 3 verified facts across at least 2 sub-dimensions, and its rationale must cite them by ID.
method.who_did_what: Facts, claims, quotes, scores and rationales were written by Claude Code (an LLM agent) as judgment. Code fetched the public sources, mapped signals, checked coverage, verified every quote, enforced the scoring rules, and wrote these files. No code checks that a fact means what its claim says; that needs a human reader.

limits: Proxy industry: fractional CFO has no NAICS code. Report figures describe management consulting (54161, a superset of the chosen 541611) or accounting (54121c, the rejected neighbor), not the niche.
Dated and mixed-vintage sources: IBISWorld May and August 2026, First Research July 2025 (one profitability figure is from 2023), while AI finance tools change monthly.
IBISWorld 54121c contradicts itself on market size and growth ($158.4bn/1.4% vs $157.4bn/1.3%); neither figure drives a score.
First Research is thin: no competitor market shares (PARTIAL/low confidence on S2), no stated industry code.
No source measures buyer concentration, switching, or substitution for $2M-$20M firms specifically; the buyer and substitute scores extrapolate from industry-wide or all-business data.
Vendor pages (Pilot, Intuit) are marketing claims, cited as claims, not as independent evidence of performance.
Two public facts are secondary or archived: the AICPA 2025 Trends figures come via CFO Dive coverage; the BLS page was fetched from its Internet Archive snapshot because bls.gov blocks scripts.
Verification proves each quote exists in its cited source; it does not prove the claim drawn from it. Scores are an LLM agent's judgment under stated rules.

forces.name: Rivalry among existing competitors
forces.rationale: Rivalry is strong: no firm leads (R1, top firm 5.3%), over 80% of establishments are one-person shops (R2), a listed rival calls the market highly fragmented (R3, R4), and growth is slowing to about 1% a year (R5, R8), so firms grow by taking each other's clients. Accounting firms that already hold the small-business relationship are moving into advisory (R6), and a funded rival publishes a $1,750/month entry price that anchors buyers (R12). It is a 4 and not a 5 because niche specialists can still hold price (R9) and First Research reads accounting as more concentrated than IBISWorld does (R10), so a vertical-focused fractional CFO faces less head-on rivalry than a generic one.

forces.name: Bargaining power of buyers
forces.rationale: Individually our buyers are weak: there are 36.2 million US small businesses and no customer class or single client dominates (B1, B2, B3), and IBISWorld's 'high' rating comes from large corporations our $2M-$20M segment does not include (B8). Collectively they still cap price, because each client can leave cheaply and at will (B4, B5), shops on the price of basic services (B6), can bring the work in-house by hiring a controller (B7), and cuts discretionary retainers in a slow economy (B10). I was torn between 2 and 3 and chose 3 because low switching costs make keeping clients, not winning them, the constant pressure on a retainer business, even with the advice dependence noted in B9.

forces.name: Bargaining power of suppliers
forces.rationale: The supplier that matters is senior finance talent, and it is scarce and getting scarcer: demand has outrun new accountants (P1), graduates fell 6.6% (P2), employers compete for about 115,300 openings a year (P4), and wages are the largest cost line (P3). Suppliers can also forward-integrate: a senior person who leaves takes the revenue (P5), and the main small-business software vendor is building forecasting and KPI analysis into its own product (P6). It is a 4 and not a 5 because part-time talent pools, which are the fractional model itself, are the standard mitigation (P7), and supply should ease as enrollment rises and more states relax the 150-hour rule (P8).

forces.name: Threat of substitutes
forces.rationale: Substitutes are real for the lower layer of the work: ERP and analytics software (X1), free generative-AI analysis (X2), do-it-yourself tools (X3) and Intuit's bookkeeping agent (X4), and a listed provider warns that technology lets its own clients bypass it (X5). The judgment layer, deciding what to do with the numbers, is harder to replace: software needs a specialist overseeing it (X6), IBISWorld rates DIY accounting as low (X7), only 7.6% of businesses used AI in the latest federal survey (X8), and Bench's sudden shutdown shows the risk of replacing a person with a platform (X9). I was torn between 3 and 4 because the AI evidence is mostly vendor claims about a fast-moving category, and I chose 3 based on current adoption data.

overall_read.text: This is a moderately unattractive industry for a new fractional CFO firm. Two linked forces dominate it: the threat of new entrants and rivalry. With no capital or licence gate, every experienced finance professional is a potential competitor, which keeps the field fragmented, slow-growing and anchored on price. Supplier power over senior talent adds pressure on the cost side and feeds the same problem, because the people we would hire can set up on their own. Buyer power and substitutes matter less, so our profits will depend on firm-level differentiation, such as a vertical niche and sticky client relationships, rather than on industry structure.

least_confident.why: The evidence conflicts and is weak where it matters most. IBISWorld rates DIY accounting as low (X7), while the management-consulting report and a listed rival treat AI and software as active threats (X2, X5). The strongest evidence of substitute performance is vendor marketing (X4, and P6 on the supplier side), not data on what buyers actually do. The only adoption number (X8) covers all US businesses and all uses of AI, not finance work at $2M-$20M firms. The reports are also from 2025-2026, while AI finance tools change month to month, and the industry itself is a proxy.
least_confident.what_would_settle_it: Three things would settle it: (1) Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey AI-use data cut by firm size and by business function (finance or accounting), to see whether $2M-$20M firms use AI for planning and forecasting, not just for marketing copy; (2) 10-20 interviews with owners in the target band who have recently dropped or skipped outside CFO help, asking what replaced it; (3) adoption or retention numbers for products like Intuit's Finance Agent among mid-market users, if Intuit discloses them. If those show software replacing the forecasting and decision-support work, not just bookkeeping, the score should go to 4.

stage1_mapping.why: Industry growth rate is a rivalry sub-dimension: 1.0%/yr forecast growth means share is won from rivals; size/growth is also what attracts entrants.
Growth rate again (rivalry). This is the report that contradicts itself ($158.4bn/1.4% vs $157.4bn/1.3%); both are kept and neither is used for a score.
133,000 establishments = number of competitors (rivalry: fragmentation); the 4%/yr forecast is the growth sub-dimension.
'Entry of niche firms ... expected to increase' is direct evidence on entry; more niche entrants then raise rivalry.
Cloud/SaaS/AI adoption by small accounting FIRMS lowers the cost of operating a small practice (entry), not a tool clients use instead (so not substitutes).
'Slow economy cuts business needs' is the demand-trend sub-dimension of buyer power; the litigation-risk quote for firms that act as consultants is a (weak) entry barrier.
